title: Visiting an Iranian home
goal: Spend a whole evening as a guest in an Iranian home — from taking off your shoes to knowing when it's time to leave — without a single awkward step.
bekal: greet your hosts and their family the right way
praise, refuse, and accept food in just the right measure
know when and how to say goodbye

dialogs.title: گفتگو — شامِ جمعه
dialogs.intro: Friday night, half past eight. Budi arrives at Maryam's family home carrying a box of pastries.

notes: ⚠️ **Here بکشید means "help yourself (to food)", not "pull".** Literally کشیدن means "to pull", but with food it means serving yourself onto your plate. غذا بکشید ("help yourself to food"), برنج بکشید ("have some rice"). The same verb is also used for smoking (سیگار کشیدن) and drawing (نقاشی کشیدن).

⚠️ **"Don't be shy" = تعارف نکنید, literally "don't do taarof".** This is the most direct use of the word تعارف: the host is asking you to stop the polite back-and-forth and really eat. When you hear this, it means you've refused enough — now you can accept.

⚠️ **Don't praise one object too much.** If you call a vase, a scarf, or a painting beautiful twice in a row, there's a real chance your host will offer it to you as a پیشکش ("gift") — and refusing it becomes a long affair. Praise it once, warmly, then move on.
**A سفره is a cloth spread on the floor for meals.** Many Iranian families eat on the floor around a sofre rather than at a table. سرِ سفره means "at the meal", and has nothing to do with heads.

**"I'll take my leave" = مرخص شوم**, literally "may I be dismissed". The polite way to leave someone's home. Lighter options: دیگر رفع زحمت کنیم ("let's end this bother for you") or simply دیگر باید برویم.

**A very respectful "come" = تشریف بیاورید.** The word تشریف ("honor") forms polite verbs: تشریف بیاورید ("please come"), تشریف بیاورید تو ("please come in"), تشریف داشته باشید ("please stay"). You don't need to use it, but you'll hear it.

grammars.title: One evening, from door to door

Persian
Say it
Meaning
rows: This is just a little something

after: **Send a message the next morning.** It's not a custom written in any book, but it works: a line of thanks the next day almost guarantees a second invitation. Unit 20 teaches you how to write it.

grammars.title: Praising the right way
after: ⚠️ **Praise for someone's child always comes with ماشاءالله.** Praising without it — "what a healthy child", "what a pretty child" — is believed to invite bad luck. The same habit is common across much of the Muslim world.
**Praising the hosts is safer than praising their things.** Praise their cooking, their hospitality, the warmth of their home — none of that can be given to you. The blue vase in the corner can.

head: Persian
Say it
What it is
rows: crispy rice crust from the bottom of the pot

blocks.text: **Everyone at an Iranian table fights over the ته‌دیگ.** The golden rice crust from the bottom of the pot — sometimes with potato or bread underneath — is considered the best part and served separately on its own plate. If your host offers it to you, that's not تعارف: it's an honor. Accept.

⚠️ **About shaking hands:** between men and women who aren't family, handshakes don't always happen. A safe rule for men: **don't offer your hand first to a woman**; if she offers hers, take it. If not, place your right hand on your chest and bow slightly — a polite, warm gesture that's welcome everywhere.

blocks.title: A plate of fresh herbs: سبزی خوردن
items: Almost every big Iranian meal comes with a plate of fresh raw herbs: نعناع (mint), ریحان (basil), ترخون (tarragon), جعفری (parsley), تره (chives), alongside کاهو (lettuce), تربچه (radishes), and a piece of پنیر (white cheese).
How to eat it: take a piece of bread, add cheese and a handful of herbs, roll it up, eat. Anyone who grew up with fresh herb plates — in Vietnam, Lebanon, or Southeast Asia — will feel right at home.
